brief_extract:
JANUARY, 1951

NEW YEAR — NEW ERA

ANOTHER new year means that inevitably we look back on the events of the previous twelve months and ahead to what the future has in store. In this Festival of Britain year we are casting our minds back a hundred years, over a period in which there have perhaps been the most rapid advances in all those fields of technical achievement which affect the lives of us all. These developments are the results of the scientist’s researches and the engineer’s skill; in their first application to everyday life all attention is concentrated on the sheer interest of a new process, or a new material, or with radio and television on the wonder of a whole new means of communication, and of necessity questions of design and variety of use are not closely considered.

JANUARY, 1951

NONA BAKER, a member of the E.A.W. Headquarters staff, relates some of her experiences during three years in Japanese-occupied Malaya. The drawing illustrates the "house" in the jungle in which she and her brother lived.

brief_context: Location of the tin mine where the author's brother worked.
brief_extract:
The drawing illustrates the "house" in the jungle in which she and her brother lived. JUNGLE SANCTUARY

IN 1935 I went out to Malaya to keep house for my brother who was manager of a large tin mine at Sungei Lembing, in the State of Pahang. When it became obvious that, sooner or later, the Japanese would attack Malaya, my brother suggested that we should live in the jungle until they were driven out.

By tremendous feats of en-
durance the guerillas managed to
attack widely separated posts on
consecutive nights, so that the

brief_context: Place where narrator was taken after leaving the jungle.
brief_extract: We did not hear of the Japanese surrender until the end of August, when we gradually worked our way out of the jungle. On September 11th I was taken into Kuantan and delivered to the care of Colonel Spencer Chapman, the author of "The Jungle is Neutral." He and the other members of Force 136 who were with him helped me tremendously in the rather difficult task of re- adjustment after so long a period of isolation. After a short stay in Kuantan I moved over to Kuala Lumpur, where I received the first news of my family for nearly four years.

brief_context: Place where narrator received news of his family.

After a short stay in Kuantan I moved over to Kuala Lumpur, where I received the first news of my family for nearly four years. In the middle of November I began a long and rather dis- jointed journey to England, which I reached on December 30th, 1945, four years to the day almost since I had gone into the jungle.

brief_context: Location of the Rinso Wash Testing Laboratories.
brief_extract: Nowadays it has become a cliché to say that housewives have the "marvels of modern science" at their disposal, and though this is taken for granted, it is still very interesting to see scientific testing directly applied to goods of particular interest to them. Paying a visit to the Rinso Wash Testing Laboratories at Port Sunlight, Cheshire, affords a glimpse of many aspects of this scientific testing. Manufacturers producing fabrics treated by the well-known "Sanforized " shrunk process, send them to be fully tested in the laboratories to verify that the process has been carried out correctly and that garments carrying an identifying label will live up to their claim of no shrinkage.

Education — A Changing Concept

By PHYLLIS THOMPSON

Housecraft Room, with small dining room leading from it

OF all the developments which
stand out today in sharp con-
trast to the position in the last
hundred years, technical educa-
tion for girls is one of the most
noteworthy. This new concept of
secondary technical education is
seen in really practical form in the
West Ham County Technical
School for Girls. This school is
one of the first of its kind in the
country, and is situated in one of
the largest industrial areas, where
there is a long tradition of techni-
cal education for boys.

A Developing Story

THIS issue of The Electrical Age is one of contrasts, but, like the South Bank Exhibition itself, it shows how the old has contributed to the new, for the present age is a part of an envolv-ing story. The comforts and advantages of modern living are the results of the developing creative power and application of men and women who have not forgotten the aesthetic heritage of this country, while they are fully alive to all that science and engineering have to offer to the lives of the people.

brief_extract:
The Mansion House
Burlington preached and insisted on the validity of absolute classical standards in architecture, and this firm conviction influenced architecture in England for nearly a century, and perhaps still does so, for nearly every modern public building shows portico and columns generally of the Ionic (or ramshorn) pattern. Kent seems to have excelled in decoration, and it is likely that he is responsible for the interior of the State Room in the Mansion House here, built in 1725-6, one of the earliest official residences for a Chief Citizen and 30 years older than the Mansion House in London. The reception rooms were the main consideration in the construction of these houses, and the result is that there is a magnificent State Room on the first floor - the full width of the house - one of the finest early Georgian rooms in England.

brief_context: Region where wool clothing practice continued until 19th century.
brief_extract: Laundry was such an important craft that the men who superintended the king’s laundry were important High Court officials. Wool was the fabric mostly used for clothing in ancient Rome, and this practice continued throughout Europe practically until the nineteenth century. Wool was prepared for wearing, and cleaned when dirty by a Guild known as the Fullers; these men trampled on the cloth in running water, using fuller’s earth to cause the wool to mat together, or felt, so that a strong heavy fabric was made.

Lawton, Birming-
ham President, summed up this
feast of colour in a telling phrase:
“One’s first glimpse of the fields
reminds one of our great grand-
mothers’ patchwork quilts, but
more brilliant.”
To continue the reminiscences:
“Words will never express
exactly the breathtaking experi-
ence of a visit to the flower
market—flowers of every colour
and hue piled in their thousands
with scents intermingling; auctions
taking place in absolute silence;
and busy porters moving six-foot,
three-tier trolleys loaded with
flowers and plants. The market
was intersected with canals, all
under cover, where boats were re-
ceiving cargoes of flowers for
their journeys all over Europe
and even destined to fly to our
own country. The tour of the canals linked
up the tour of flower fields, and
illustrated how much the water-
ways serve both as methods of
transport without any bustle or
crush, and also keep the land
well watered.”
Perhaps the most interesting
part of the short trip was the
meeting with the Dutch E.A.W.

brief_extract: I have mentioned only two of the notable buildings of this gracious age, but they are of early date and it would be difficult to find others exactly like them. OCTOBER, 1951

Electricity at Home and Abroad

THIS summer has indeed seen much “electrical activity” in Festival and Conference, in celebrations in city and town, and in county and village shows. Many people have also seen in other countries the marvels wrought by electricity in ways not applicable here, such as the funicular railways of the Alps, and have enjoyed the cleanliness of travel in long-distance electric trains. They have appreciated what the harnessing of the mountains of Europe has meant in the plentiful supply of hydro-electric power—the “white coal,” as it is called in Norway.

THE ELECTRICAL AGE. OCTOBER, 1951

The Liverpool Festival, 1951

By RITA BROWN, Honorary Secretary, Liverpool and District
E.A.W. Branch

Liverpool in festive mood

(“Liverpool Echo”)

THE Liverpool Festival is over!

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of the Festival of Britain.
brief_extract: The City looked lovely in her festive frock, flowers and decorative trees in great profusion, carnival bunting, bright new paintwork, and especially the flags, for is there a lovelier sight than the Union Jack (or better still, Union Jacks) flying proudly in the breeze? Liverpool gladly accepted the invitation to become a regional arts festival centre for the Festival of Britain, and was supported by local authorities and other bodies. As an Arts Festival it can be said that the Liverpool Festival maintained the best traditions.

location_standardised: Liverpool Cathedral, Liverpool, Merseyside, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: The location for the opening service of the festival.
brief_extract: Those who find pleasure in the arts have, through the Liverpool Festival, had opportunities which rarely come the way of those who live outside the metropolitan area, but perhaps the real triumph of the Liverpool Festival was that it became very much a festival of the people, and not merely a festival for the people—a festival with something doing for everyone, and everyone doing something. In true British fashion the Festival opened with an impressive and dignified service in our beautiful Cathedral, with a most inspiring Address by the Archbishop of York. On each of the three Sundays special services, with visiting clergy, were held.

MUCH of the lighting of the South Bank Exhibition is straightforward enough. That is not to say that it is not good—a great deal of it is very good in- deed; but it is quite obvious to the observer how it is done, and how the desired effect was achieved.

brief_extract: That is not to say that it is not good—a great deal of it is very good in- deed; but it is quite obvious to the observer how it is done, and how the desired effect was achieved. In this category I would place the famous concourse lights, which, recessed into the pavement, make one think one is treading the starry floor of Heaven itself, the underwater floodlighting of the great waterfall and fountains by the Skylon, and the excellent floodlighting of murals and statuary throughout the exhibi- tion. Some of the ways in which some other effects have been produced are not so easily discovered, and it is the purpose of this article to explain them to you so that, if anyone talks of them, you may be in the position of the member of the audience at a conjuring show, who infuriates the enter- tainer but derives great personal satisfaction by explaining to the audience exactly how each trick is done.

It is this

Almost everywhere you go in
the South Bank and at Battersea
Park, you will see the use of
“black light.” It is best used, I
consider, in Schweppes’ Grotto in
Battersea Park, where at the end
of one’s journey through the Cave
of the Winds, the Cavern of Fire,
and the grotto of the leaping foun-
tain, one passes through “under-
water” chasms where fish and sea
creatures gleam mysteriously out
of dark crevices in the rocks. This
is achieved by means of a special
type of high-pressure mercury
discharge lamp with a black glass
bulb, which allows only long-wave
ultra violet to pass through it,
and traps all visible light.

the physical, mental and spiritual
development of human beings

in communities.
